description.value: Participants viewed neutral faces and received audio prompts to think positive, think negative, or look at the image.

spans.text: Across four runs that were each 480 seconds in length, 40 faces were presented: 16 were presented with instructions to “Think Positive”; 16 were presented with instructions to “Think Negative”; and eight additional trials were presented with instructions to “Look” at the image to reduce predictability.

description.value: The first four seconds of each 10-second neutral-face trial, before the cognitive-reappraisal audio prompt; participants viewed the face without a positive or negative reappraisal instruction.

spans.text: 4 s after image onset, audio prompts to either “Think Positive” or “Think Negative” signaled the participant to engage a specific cognitive reappraisal strategy.

description.value: The six-second post-instruction phase after the audio prompt Think Positive; participants reinterpreted the neutral face as someone they liked, liked them, or was kind and friendly to enhance positive emotional responses.

spans.text: Specifically, participants were instructed that to “think positive” about a face, they should imagine the picture is of someone they are interested in, whom they really like, who really likes them, or who is a kind and friendly person.

description.value: The six-second post-instruction phase after the audio prompt Think Negative; participants reinterpreted the neutral face as someone hostile or someone they disliked to enhance negative emotional responses.

spans.text: To “think negative” about a face, they were instructed to imagine that the picture is of someone hostile or whom they don’t like.

Stimuli were presented using E-Prime software v. 2.0 (Psychology Software Tools Inc., Pittsburgh, PA).

stimuli.value: Neutral closed-mouth images from the NimStim set.

spans.text: Faces were neutral closed-mouth images from the NimStim set ( Tottenham et al., 2009 ).

instructions.value: Participants viewed neutral faces and, four seconds after image onset, heard an instruction to think positive or think negative about the face. For think positive, they reinterpreted the person as someone they liked, liked them, or was kind and friendly; for think negative, they imagined the person was hostile or someone they disliked. They were instructed not to look away, distract themselves, or close their eyes.

spans.text: Trials began with a 1-s fixation coupled with an orienting tone, after which a face was presented for 10 s. 4 s after image onset, audio prompts to either “Think Positive” or “Think Negative” signaled the participant to engage a specific cognitive reappraisal strategy.
